claims.claim: Many English grammar courses use eight traditional parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection.
A noun commonly names a person, place, thing, or idea; a pronoun can replace a noun; and a verb can express action, occurrence, or state.
Adjectives modify nouns or pronouns, adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, and conjunctions connect units such as words, phrases, or clauses.
The same spelling can function as different parts of speech in different sentences, so classification should be based on role in context rather than memorizing a word's isolated label.
Some grammar treatments count articles separately or analyze them as a type of adjective, so the inventory of categories reflects a chosen descriptive framework.
Pronoun reference can be unclear when a reader cannot determine the intended antecedent, and revision can make the reference explicit.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether English has eight or nine parts of speech and how articles should be treated.
positions: Business Grammar presents eight parts of speech.
Language Foundations Handbook presents nine and describes articles as a type of adjective.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the common eight-part classroom model while explicitly explaining that article treatment varies by grammar framework.
